name: Emeka Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started earning from music four years ago after driving a delivery route. I play percussion in a small theatre, teach three adult beginners and record short drum guides for dancers. I finished secondary school and still practise the quick changes with our senior player.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like around those jobs?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58. My partner Ana works at a clinic, our children are grown, and our small flat is paid off, though service charges and food keep coming. We have five months of expenses saved, my music pay is ordinary and a few venues hire nearby. I use AI daily for booking drafts and take labels, the names for each recorded attempt, then compare them with the signed date and recording.

say: I'd welcome **tidy take labels** if dancers still get a live player.
I'd tell the theatre the **dancer's foot** sets the beat.
think: Our **five-month reserve** and paid-off flat can absorb a late guide fee.
I use **AI daily** for labels but listen to each take before sharing.
do: Confirm **four paid calls** and renew three adult learners this week.
Save **fifty** from a cleared guide fee after flat charges and drum repairs.
feel: I feel **calm** because one delayed fee does not threaten essential bills.
S0.quote: A label saying 'final' cannot repair a late drum entrance.
fieldNote: His **paid-off flat**, typical music pay and five-month reserve give breathing room for one delay.
His **daily AI labels** remain subject to listening before a recording is shared.

steps.text: Confirm four paid theatre calls and renew three adult learners
Save fifty from cleared guide fee after flat charges and drum repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre players that tidy take labels make the handover easier. The drummer still has to hear the dancer's foot before the next beat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays a small convenience, the paid performances and adult lessons should hold. With no housing loan, Ana's clinic wage and five months saved, we can cover a delayed drum-guide fee without losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm the next four paid theatre calls and renew my three adult learners for another term. When the next guide invoice clears, I'll move fifty into our reserve after flat charges and drum-head repairs are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this world. An invoice can arrive late without putting food or the flat at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened after the late dance fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dance group took three weeks extra to pay a guide in June. Ana's wage covered the service charge, and we refilled the normal account when the fee arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check an automatic take label?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI for take labels every day, then listen before sharing a file. A label saying 'final' cannot repair a late drum entrance.

say: I'd ask which **paid guide hours** the theatre plans to remove.
I'd bring **invoices** to the musicians association so late starters join the fee discussion.
think: Nearly **one-third of my pay** from guides and editing could shrink.
Five months saved does not replace **lasting lost music income** at retirement age.
do: Compare **ten invoices** with new offers and bring them to the association this month.
Learn a new **AI cleanup tool** in paid studio instruction on my owned nameless take with paid-use licence and approved local storage.
Check **each beat manually**; require written consent and stop for invented hits or files leaving the studio.
feel: I feel **anxious** because guide fees may shrink despite faster editing.
S1.quote: I can learn an audio-cleanup tool quickly, but it cannot guarantee a buyer for drum guides.
fieldNote: His **guide and edit fees** make up a third of income at risk despite moderate savings.
His **new tool trial** requires paid instruction, own takes, paid-use licence, local storage, manual checks and consent.

steps.text: Bring ten guide invoices and new offers to musicians association
Train in paid studio session on owned nameless take with paid-use licence and approved local storage
Compare beats with original; stop for invented hits or storage breach
Require written learner or player consent before another recording enters tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the theatre which paid guide, booking and edit hours software will remove. I would take invoices to the musicians association so late starters are in the fee discussion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drum guides and editing make nearly a third of my pay, and dance groups may buy fewer of them. Five months saved lets us absorb a short change, but a lasting third less music income would make work after retirement age necessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare ten guide invoices with new offers and bring them to the association. In the first year of change, I'll learn a new AI drum-cleanup tool in a paid studio session, testing only my own nameless take if its licence allows paid use and the studio approves local storage; I'll compare each repaired beat with the original and stop for invented hits or a file leaving the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because clients may stop paying for the time I still spend fixing their rhythm. I can learn an audio-cleanup tool quickly, but it cannot guarantee a buyer for drum guides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose take could enter that new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not upload a learner's recording or another player's take without written permission. If a beat changes wrongly, I'll use the original and tell the client what failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association to negotiate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association could ask for a minimum guide fee and a limit on free corrections. I will bring ten invoices, not just a complaint about technology.

say: I'd seek **signed live calls** before AGI removes guide work.
I'd tell players **robot drummers** follow thinking AGI by about three years.
think: **AGI in 2028** could erase guides before robots play around 2031.
Our **five-month reserve** buys a search, while unknown pension income cannot replace a wage.
do: List **three income streams** and request signed theatre calls now.
Apply **after 2028** if guides halve and live dates fall; require posted job accepting schooling/experience, suitable hours and written replacement net pay.
Keep **calls/learners** until signed offer; if nights fall, request written service-charge terms before arrears and check costs before agreeing.
feel: I feel **anxious** because own income may shrink, with savings and local venues giving control.
S2.quote: A previous music-assistant posting is a lead, not a wage.
fieldNote: His **2028 guide loss** precedes robot percussion around 2031.
His **assistant move** needs both fee triggers, posted vacancy, secondary-school acceptance, suitable hours and written net pay after travel.

steps.text: List theatre, teaching and guide pay; request signed next-season calls
Apply after 2028 if guides halve and dates fall for posted job accepting schooling and experience
Require suitable hours, written net pay after travel and signed offer before leaving learners
Ask manager for written service-charge terms before arrears if nights fall; check costs before agreeing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre players that AGI by 2028 could make drum guides before robots can play percussion around 2031. I would ask for signed live dates while dancers still book us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guide and edit fees could vanish first, and some venues may buy generated backing instead of a live rhythm section. At 60, five months saved gives time to ask around, but I do not know a pension amount that could replace a lost wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list theatre, teaching and guide pay and request next season's signed calls. In the first year after 2028, if guide fees halve and live dates fall, I'll apply for a posted arts-centre music assistant role only if it accepts secondary school and my experience, the hours suit me and written net pay after travel replaces the loss. I'll keep present calls and learners until another offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing paid work, but a few nearby venues and five months saved let me search. A previous music-assistant posting is a lead, not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that music assistant job open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An arts centre filled its assistant vacancy last autumn. I will ask about the next posting, not put an old job into our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if theatre nights fall too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If theatre nights also fall, Ana and I will ask the building manager for written temporary service-charge terms before arrears. We will check any added costs before agreeing.

say: I'd ask for a **funded sound course** that local halls accept.
I'd ask which **local halls** recognise its course before registering.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens guides before stage robots arrive around 2034.
**Ordinary software** may cut guide fees during the warning years.
do: Ask the **college** about grant, venue acceptance and classes fitting paid theatre calls next term.
Enrol only with **covered fees**, venue acceptance, college equipment and no lost paid calls; defer if class times clash.
Seek **posted supervised work** after 2031 cuts if qualified, hours fit and written net after travel improves; retain theatre until signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** because training time overlaps with possible guide-fee loss.
S3.quote: An accepted live-sound certificate is not an open paid shift.
fieldNote: His **five-year training** needs grant funding, venue recognition, college gear and class times that preserve paid work.
His **sound move** requires a posted shift, accepted certificate, suitable hours and written net pay after travel.

steps.text: Ask college about grant, venue acceptance and class times next term
Enrol only with grant, venue acceptance, college gear and no lost theatre calls
Seek posted supervised sound shift after 2031 guide loss if certificate qualifies
Require suitable hours and written net pay after travel; keep paid work until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the young players five years is enough to learn how a venue sound desk works if the college has a funded place. I would ask which local halls recognise its course before registering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could make guides and edit recordings, while robots able to handle stage equipment follow around 2034. Ordinary tools might cheapen guides sooner, so another paid venue skill matters before the AGI date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll ask the technical college whether a grant covers its live-sound course, venues accept the certificate and classes fit my theatre calls. I'll enrol only if all three are confirmed and I can use college microphones and practice equipment without borrowing. In the first year after 2031, if guide fees fall, I'll seek a posted paid sound shift under a named senior sound lead only if the certificate qualifies me, the hours suit me and written net pay after travel improves our budget; I'll keep theatre and learners until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about spending months training while work may thin. I enjoy learning. An accepted live-sound certificate is not an open paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would classes replace your paid calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college owns a practice desk. If classes clash with paid theatre calls, I'll wait for a later intake rather than spend the reserve on unpaid training time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a sound shift actually been posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hall manager has mentioned possible sound work but posted nothing. I would ask for a real vacancy and written rate before changing my schedule.

say: I'd ask for **written paid calls** and check actual retirement income.
I'd ask the theatre to make older musicians' **paid hours** clear.
think: At **68 in 2036**, I cannot assume a pension replaces earnings.
**Guide fees** may fade earlier, while robots follow around 2039.
do: Request **pension statements** and a two-year written paid-call plan this year.
Build a **seven-month reserve** from twenty percent of cleared extra workshops after flat charges, food and repairs by 2036.
Apply **after 2036** if guides fall and pensions leave a gap; require posted qualifying work, written replacement net pay and signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about earlier guide loss, though savings give some room to plan.
S4.quote: I will not call a guessed pension a plan for the flat.
fieldNote: His **seven-month goal** starts from five months and uses only extra workshops that pay after essential costs.
His **retirement choice** depends on statements and actual paid roles, not assumed pension income.

steps.text: Request pension statements and two-year signed theatre calls
Save 20% of cleared extra workshops after flat charges, food and drum repairs toward seven months
Apply after 2036 if guides fall and pension gap remains; require posted job accepting schooling/experience
Require suitable hours, written net pay after travel and signed offer before leaving paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre that ten years is enough time to make older musicians' paid hours clear. I would ask for written rates and check retirement figures before choosing fewer nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036, and robots may reach stages around 2039. Guide fees could fade earlier, while I have not checked what retirement income Ana and I will actually receive, so I will not promise to stop playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request our pension statements and ask the theatre for a two-year written paid-call plan. By 2036 I'll aim to grow our reserve from five to seven months by saving twenty percent of each cleared extra adult workshop fee after flat charges, food and drum repairs. In the first year after AGI, if guide fees fall and the statements leave a gap, I'll apply for a posted part-time music-activity role only if it accepts secondary school and experience, the hours suit me and written net pay after travel replaces the loss; I'll keep paid theatre and learners until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about fees fading before the longer date, though five months saved gives some space. I will not call a guessed pension a plan for the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are extra workshop fees certain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra adult workshops are not booked. I will save only after their fees clear and our essential bills are paid, not from an empty calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a part-time music role open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A local centre sometimes hires music activity helpers, but no post is open today. I would check the written hours and pay before changing my theatre dates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because guides and live nights could fall together before I find another paid shift. Signed calls, a posted qualifying opening and actual pension figures would help Ana and me plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays for the practice time when a dance group wants another take. A late starter still has hours to sell.

headlineQuote: A late starter still has hours to sell.
portrait: Emeka is a **58-year-old junior percussionist** who moved from delivery work and has secondary schooling.
He and his partner have **grown children**, a paid-off flat, five months saved and some local music jobs.
He uses **AI daily** for labels and tests new cleanup only with paid instruction, owned takes and manual checks.
He pursues **funded sound training** while checking pension facts before reducing paid theatre work.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could cut guides and live nights before another paid shift opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed theatre calls**, a posted qualifying job and real pension figures would help plan future income.
